newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ninety-five states back milestone landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: Ninety-five states back milestone landmine ban.

text.p: Ninety-five countries agreed on Friday to sign up to a ban on landmines, twice as many as organisers of a conference in Brussels had expected.
The first ever treaty to ban the use, production, stockpiling and transfer of landmines is due to be signed in Ottawa in December.
"The Brussels Declaration is a milestone on the road to a complete ban," Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Derycke said in a speech to delegates at the end of the four-day conference.
Belgium, the first country to ban mines unilaterally, in March 1995, hosted the conference which continued a series of discussions started in Ottawa in October 1996.

Belgian officials had said before the meeting they hoped 45 countries would sign the declaration, a pre-condition for joining talks in September in Oslo, where the final wording of the treaty will be negotiated.

"It is the immense human suffering caused by anti-personnel mines which has brought delegations of so many countries to Brussels," Princess Astrid, a member of Belgium's royal family, said in a speech.
Every year, mines kill about 26,000 people and maim thousands more for life.

A total of 115 countries took part in the talks. Another 37 were present as observers, including Cuba, India, Indonesia, Iran, Israel, Libya, the Palestinian Authority, Russia, Turkey and the United States.
"This is a historic result. More than half of the countries in the world have agreed to sign the ban," Cornelio Sommaruga, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, told reporters.
During the conference and in the weeks before it, some two dozen new governments committed themselves to signing the treaty, including France, Spain, Italy, Britain and Brazil.
Angola and Bosnia, two of the world's most mine-infested countries, also signed up.
Non-governmental groups campaigning against mines said hoped the Brussels text would not be weakened in Oslo.
"We must remain true to the draft text. We want a treaty without loopholes or exceptions," Human Rights Watch arms project director Stephen Goose told reporters.

The most notable absentee from the Brussels Declaration was the United States, which attended as an observer and did not sign because it favours separate talks at the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva.

The Geneva talks, which require consensus, are not expected to produce a landmine ban for some years, although a special co-ordinator on the subject of land mines was appointed on Thursday in an attempt to detach the issue from deadlocked nuclear topics.
"The Geneva conference is a forum for recalcitrant states," Jody Williams, head of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told Reuters.
The ICBL says the United States, Greece and Turkey are now the only NATO countries not on board the Ottawa talks.
But Derycke played down rivalry between the two diplomatic efforts. "The two processes can complement each other. If something positive comes from Geneva, all the better," he said.
